opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at a tension that runs through a lot of retrieval work right now.

The way I think about it is that chunk size is really a decision about where you want the "understanding" to happen. With small chunks, you're betting that the retriever and whatever structure you build on top of it can do a lot of the work. In HippoRAG, that's the whole point. We break things into passages, extract entities and relationships, and build a graph that acts like an index. A memory system then links pieces of information that may never appear together in a single document. The small units are what make that associative structure possible. If your units are huge, the graph gets muddy, because one node is connected to everything.

LongRAG starts from a different observation: long-context models have gotten much better at reading. So why fragment the corpus into tiny pieces, force the retriever to find the needle, and lose context at the chunk boundaries? If you group documents into much larger retrieval units, you need far fewer of them, recall goes up, and you hand the reader model a coherent body of text it can reason over. That shifts work from retrieval to reading.

So the tradeoff is roughly precision and structure versus context and simplicity. Small chunks give you fine-grained control and let you do multi-hop association across sources efficiently. But you risk losing local context, and you depend on the retriever getting a lot right. Large units are more forgiving, and they keep the narrative intact. But you pay in cost and latency, and you're trusting the reader not to get distracted by a lot of irrelevant text. That's still a real issue even with very capable long-context models.

I don't see them as competing philosophies so much as points on a spectrum, and I think the right answer depends on the task. If your question needs connecting facts scattered across many documents that don't reference each other, that's where structured, fine-grained indexing like HippoRAG shines. If the answer mostly lives within one or a few related documents and the challenge is reading them well, consolidating makes a lot of sense.

Longer term, I suspect the interesting systems will combine both: something like an associative index over fine-grained knowledge that decides *what* to pull in, then hands much larger, context-rich spans to a strong reader. That's closer to how human memory seems to work anyway. You have cues that trigger associations, and then you reconstruct the fuller episode around them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a really good question, and it's something we thought about quite a bit when we were designing HippoRAG. So the way I see it, the tradeoff is really about where you want the burden of integration to sit — on the retriever or on the reader.

With LongRAG, the idea is basically: modern LLMs have these huge context windows, so why bother with fine-grained retrieval at all? Just group documents into these big units, retrieve a handful of them, and let the model sort things out. And honestly, that works surprisingly well for a lot of cases. If the information you need is co-located — it's in the same document or the same Wikipedia page cluster — then the long-context model can just read it all and figure out the answer. You avoid a lot of the brittleness that comes from chunking, like splitting a sentence in the middle of an important fact, or losing the context that tells you what "he" or "the company" is referring to.

But the thing we were really focused on with HippoRAG is a different kind of problem, which is multi-hop, knowledge-integration questions where the pieces of evidence are spread across documents that aren't co-located at all. They're not in the same cluster, they might not even be lexically similar to each other. The classic example is something like, "which Stanford professor works on the neuroscience of Alzheimer's" — where you've got one passage about a professor at Stanford, another one about their work on Alzheimer's, and no single chunk connects them. LongRAG doesn't really help you there, because consolidating documents doesn't bring those two things together unless they happen to be grouped already. And you can't just put the whole corpus in context, at least not at the scales we care about.

So the way HippoRAG handles it is kind of inspired by how the hippocampus works, at least at a very abstract level. You take small passages, you extract entities and relations with an LLM into this knowledge graph — that's the pattern separation side, you're keeping things sparse and distinct — and then at retrieval time you run Personalized PageRank from the query entities, and that spreads activation across the graph. That's the pattern completion part. The nice thing is that the graph does the integration for you, so even if the two relevant passages are far apart in embedding space, they can be connected through a shared entity node, and you pull them both back in a single retrieval step. And we found that this actually makes a huge difference on those multi-hop benchmarks, and it's also much cheaper than iterative approaches like IRCoT, because you're not doing multiple rounds of LLM calls at query time.

Now, the honest downside of small chunks is exactly what LongRAG is reacting to. When you break things into passages, you lose context. The entity extraction can be noisy — the LLM might miss a coreference, or produce slightly different surface forms for the same entity that we then have to reconcile with the synonymy edges. And if you retrieve a passage in isolation, the reader sometimes doesn't have enough surrounding context to use it well.

So I actually don't think these are mutually exclusive. I kind of see them as complementary. You could imagine building the graph over smaller units, because that's where you get the precision for the hippocampal-style indexing, but then at read time, expanding back out to larger units — the full document or a bigger neighborhood — so the reader gets the context that LongRAG benefits from. The graph gives you the "where to look" across the corpus, and the long context gives you the "read it properly once you're there." In a lot of ways, that's probably where things are headed. The chunk size is less of a fundamental choice and more of a knob, and the real question is how you do the associative step across the corpus, which is something that just concatenating documents doesn't solve by itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the tradeoff is really about retrieval precision versus preserving context. With small chunks, you can retrieve something very specific to the question, but you risk separating it from information you need to interpret it. With larger units, you preserve those relationships, but you also bring in more irrelevant information and ask the reader model to figure out what matters.

The idea with HippoRAG is that small retrieval units don’t necessarily have to be isolated. The graph gives us a way to connect information across those units. So you can keep retrieval relatively fine-grained while still using broader relationships to identify relevant evidence.

I wouldn’t say one approach is universally better. If the answer depends on understanding a coherent stretch of a document, keeping that context together makes sense. If you need to connect evidence scattered across documents, the connections become particularly valuable. And those choices can be complementary: you could retrieve at a fine-grained level, then provide more surrounding context to the model that generates the answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key tradeoff is between retrieval precision and preserving context. With small chunks, you can retrieve something very specific, but you risk separating it from information you need to interpret it. Keeping a whole document together preserves that context, but you may bring in a lot of material that isn’t relevant to the question.

The way I think about HippoRAG is that the graph gives us a way to connect information across those smaller units. So the retrieval unit can be small without necessarily treating each chunk as isolated. LongRAG takes a different approach: preserve more context in the retrieved unit and let the reader figure out what matters.

I don’t think one is universally better. If the answer depends on understanding a document as a whole, larger units make sense. If you need to connect specific pieces of evidence across documents, more granular retrieval can be useful. And you can combine the two: retrieve at a fine granularity, then expand the surrounding context for the reader.
